title: HTTP chunking penalty: latency vs cost scan
content:
Purpose:
This is a quick empirical scan: quantify how HTTP response chunking/streaming choices affect client-observed latency percentiles and the incremental cost (network + server CPU serialization). The goal is practical guidance for the Console/SDK and a set of low-effort mitigations we can ship.

Background / motivation:
- Many apps use streaming for UX (token-by-token or chunked).
- Streaming reduces time-to-first-byte for long outputs, but we suspect it increases p99 and CPU/network overhead due to: additional syscalls, repeated small writes, larger header overhead per chunk on some infra, TLS record framing, and less efficient gzip/deflate compression.
- We need a simple rule-of-thumb: when to stream (and how to stream) vs return full payloads.

Short takeaway (TL;DR):
- For short outputs (< ~120 tokens), single-response return is both lower median latency and lower p99; streaming offers near-zero UX benefit but costs ~5–20% more CPU/egress per request at our infra settings.
- For long outputs (> ~400 tokens), streaming reduces time-to-first-token by 40–70% and improves perceived latency for interactive UX, but increases p99 by ~15–40ms (due to tail amplification) and increases network overhead by ~8–25% depending on chunk size.
- Best immediate mitigations: 1) recommended chunk size 256–512 bytes (not tokens), 2) TLS record coalescing on server side where possible, 3) enable brotli for long streaming sessions, 4) support a lightweight header-first response (first chunk contains routing/metadata + first N tokens).

Experiment setup (short):
- Model variant: llama-13b-quant (prod-compat quant profile).
- Server: g4dn-like instance (single GPU), frontend node running nginx+uwsgi-ish proxy; measured on our staging cluster (eu-west-1).
- Workload: 10k synthetic requests, 10% warmup 90% measurement. Each request requested generation of 50 / 200 / 600 tokens (three cohorts).
- Concurrency: 100 concurrent clients (mimic web app).
- Network sim: baseline rtt ~20ms, 50 Mbps per node egress cap.
- Variants tested: single-response (full JSON at end), chunked-token (one token per chunk), chunked-fixed (256B and 1024B chunk sizes), chunked-header-first (first chunk large then streaming smaller chunks).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p99 client-observed latency to first displayed token (TTF), to final completion (TTC), server CPU for serialization (user+sys percentage), increased egress (bytes/request), TLS record count.

Representative numbers (aggregated):
Cohort A: 50-token outputs
- single-response: TTF p50=220ms, p90=310ms, p99=420ms; TTC p50=420ms; bytes/request=9.2KB; server-serialize=8% CPU
- chunked-token (one token per chunk): TTF p50=180ms, p90=260ms, p99=540ms; TTC p50=460ms; bytes/request=10.8KB; server-serialize=13% CPU
- chunked-fixed-256B: TTF p50=185ms, p90=270ms, p99=480ms; TTC p50=450ms; bytes/request=10.2KB; server-serialize=11% CPU
Notes: For short responses median TTF improves slightly with chunking, p99 worsens (small but visible) and bytes/request increases ~10–17% due to framing.

Cohort B: 200-token outputs
- single-response: TTF p50=380ms, p90=560ms, p99=980ms; TTC p50=980ms; bytes/request=36KB; server-serialize=11% CPU
- chunked-token: TTF p50=140ms, p90=200ms, p99=540ms; TTC p50=1040ms; bytes/request=41KB; server-serialize=18% CPU
- chunked-fixed-512B: TTF p50=150ms, p90=220ms, p99=480ms; TTC p50=1020ms; bytes/request=39KB; server-serialize=15% CPU
- header-first (first chunk ~1KB then 512B): TTF p50=130ms, p90=200ms, p99=450ms; TTC p50=1005ms; bytes/request=38.5KB; server-serialize=14% CPU
Notes: Streaming reduces TTF drastically (good UX), but TTC can increase slightly due to inefficiencies in many small writes; header-first is attractive (good TTF and smaller tail).

Cohort C: 600-token outputs
- single-response: TTF p50=1280ms, p90=2100ms, p99=3600ms; TTC p50=3600ms; bytes/request=110KB; server-serialize=20% CPU
- chunked-token: TTF p50=320ms, p90=580ms, p99=1500ms; TTC p50=3800ms; bytes/request=128KB; server-serialize=28% CPU
- chunked-fixed-1024B: TTF p50=350ms, p90=620ms, p99=1300ms; TTC p50=3720ms; bytes/request=122KB; server-serialize=25% CPU
- header-first: TTF p50=300ms, p90=550ms, p99=1200ms; TTC p50=3680ms; bytes/request=120KB; server-serialize=23% CPU
Notes: For very long outputs, streaming is clearly beneficial for perceived latency. The p99 improves a lot relative to single-response in TTF but absolute TTC tail remains similar; overhead bytes/request grows 8–15%.

Micro-observations (why p99 gets worse for short chunked workloads):
- TLS small-record amplification: many small writes cause more TLS records leading to more encryption throughput overhead.
- IO scheduler/epoll wakeups: small writes increase syscall rate and kernel-visible wakes on busy servers.
- Proxy buffering: some proxies add extra latency per chunk when not explicitly configured for streaming (buffering windows).
- Compression inefficiency: compressors (gzip/brotli) need some window to be effective; many tiny chunks lose compression opportunities and inflate bytes sent.

Cost model back-of-envelope (our infra numbers):
- GPU compute per long request: dominated by decode time (unchanged).
- Serialization/egress cost (per 1M requests): at p50 mix of 80% short (50 tokens), 15% medium (200 tokens), 5% long (600 tokens):
  - Single-response mix: egress ~ 9.2KB*0.8 + 36KB*0.15 + 110KB*0.05 ~= 16.9KB/request => 16.9 GB per 1M req; cost ~ $1.70 (egress @ $0.10/GB) + CPU overhead ~ equivalent to 12 vCPU-hours @$0.02/hr = $0.24 -> total ~$1.94 (very approximate)
  - Chunked-fixed-512B mix: egress ~ 18.3KB/request => 18.3 GB per 1M req; cost delta ~ +$0.13/1M req, CPU delta +~$0.10/1M req = ~+$0.23/1M requests.
Interpretation: network/CPU overhead from chunking is measurable but small in absolute $ terms at 1M req scale; however for large enterprise scale (100M+ requests) it becomes a nontrivial line item.

Recommendations (practical):
1) Default behavior: for payloads expected < ~120 tokens, use single-response. SDKs/Console should default to buffered mode unless user opts-in to streaming.
2) For streaming: recommend chunk sizes (server-side framing) of 256–1024 bytes. Avoid 1-token-per-chunk; that has worst tail and worst CPU.
3) Implement header-first pattern in SDK/proxy: first chunk includes content metadata + first N tokens (N tuned by tokenization) to minimize RTT before visible text.
4) Proxy/playground: ensure upstream proxies (nginx/Envoy) are configured with streaming-friendly flags (disable buffering, increase chunk window) and TLS record coalescing where allowed.
5) Add a cost estimator in Console that warns when streaming with small chunk size increases projected egress by >10% for a given traffic shape.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How do gRPC streaming semantics change these numbers? We need a small run with gRPC over HTTP/2 and Brotli/Deflate.
- Mobile networks: higher RTTs and smaller MTU -> chunking behavior might amplify; schedule a mobile-lab run.
- Does QUIC with coalesced datagrams eliminate most of the tail amplification? Run a QUIC-enabled staging cluster test.

Action items (next 30 days):
- [ ] Run a gRPC vs HTTP/1.1 chunking head-to-head (Omar) - target milestone 2026-04-30.
- [ ] Prototype header-first framing in the SDK (Jasmine) - 2-week spike.
- [ ] Add a Console projected-cost toggle for streaming settings (Priya + product) - spec draft.
- [ ] Note to infra: measure TLS record counts in prod (SRE ticket INF-4872).

Notes to reviewer:
- This is intentionally rough; numbers are stage-cluster-derived and vary by region/hardware. Use this doc to decide whether to change default SDK behavior and to prioritize header-first prototype.
- If you want the raw csv per-request logs (ttf, ttc, bytes, tls_records) I uploaded them to the experiment folder linked in the Jira ticket above.

Raw ascii chart (visual aid) - TTF p50 by variant (200-token cohort):
- single-response: 380ms  |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■
- chunked-512B: 150ms    |■■■■■■■■■
- header-first: 130ms    |■■■■■■■■
- chunked-token: 140ms   |■■■■■■■■■

Questions for assignees:
- Jasmine: can SDK easily implement header-first without breaking existing streaming parsers?
- Omar: can we run a quick gRPC + QUIC variant in the same staging cluster?
- Priya: would product want an explicit billing warning in Console or just a developer doc?

-- Miguel
